title: Meet Chardonnay
subtitle: The winemaker's canvas
objectives: Explain why it's called a canvas

steps.title: Many faces
steps.body: Chardonnay can taste of green apple and lemon, or peach and melon, or pineapple and mango, depending on climate. Winemaking adds butter, toast, vanilla, hazelnut or cream. Acidity ranges from high to medium, body from light to full. With Spain's Airén, it's one of the two most planted white grapes in the world.
steps.highlight: Climate sets fruit; winemaking adds the rest

steps.title: Parents and character
steps.body: DNA shows Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, probably in Burgundy in the Middle Ages. It's named after the village of Chardonnay, in the Mâconnais. Its own aromas are fairly neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking clearly. It buds early, risking frost, but ripens reliably.

steps.prompt: Why is Chardonnay called a winemaker's canvas?
options: Its own aromas are neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking
steps.explanation: Neutral fruit lets climate and winemaking choices show clearly.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Because it varies so much, look for clues: high acidity and green fruit with a chalky edge suggest cool Chablis; nutty, buttery richness with toast suggests oaked Burgundy or California; tropical fruit and soft acidity suggest a warm climate. A lack of strong aromatic signature is itself a clue.

steps.prompt: Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's a sibling of Gamay, Aligoté and Melon.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay's fruit ranges from apple to pineapple with climate
It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc from Burgundy
Its neutral character reflects site and winemaking
